title: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
summary: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them, when to open an issue before a PR, how codes of conduct are enforced, and how AI-tool policies range from labelled use (LLVM) to declining AI content (QEMU).
outcomes: Locate a project's CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT and SECURITY files using GitHub's lookup order and account defaults
Decide when to open an issue before a pull request, and compute the breakeven from a simple expected-cost model
Write issues that pass a project's forms and link PRs with closing keywords that actually close the issue
Explain the scope and enforcement ladder of the Contributor Covenant and route conduct and security reports privately
Compare LLVM, Linux kernel and QEMU policies on AI tools and write a commit that complies with each

lessons.title: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them

blocks.md: In the previous course you learned the mechanics of a pull request: fork, branch, rebase, sign off. Mechanics are only half of getting a change merged. Every project also has **norms**: written rules about what it wants, how to propose it, how people must behave, and (more and more) whether AI tools may be used. A technically perfect PR that ignores them is often closed without review.

The rules live in a small set of conventional files, which GitHub calls **community health files**. The [Open Source Guides](https://opensource.guide/how-to-contribute/) list the ones a newcomer should read first:

- `LICENSE`: the legal terms. Without one, the project is not open source.
- `README`: what the project is and how to use it.
- `CONTRIBUTING`: how to contribute, which kinds of help are wanted, and how the process works.
- `CODE_OF_CONDUCT`: how participants must behave and how violations are handled.

GitHub supports a few more: `SECURITY.md` (how to report a vulnerability), `SUPPORT.md` (where to ask for help), `FUNDING.yml` (sponsor button), plus **issue templates** in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` and a **pull request template** such as `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Templates pre-fill or structure what you type when you open an issue or PR.

scenes.caption: A CONTRIBUTING file may sit in three places in the repository itself. Names are not case sensitive. Here .gh stands for the .github folder.
If several exist, GitHub links the first one it finds in this order: the .github folder, then the root, then docs.
Nothing in .github? It checks the repository root next, then the docs folder.
Still nothing: GitHub falls back to the owner's public repository named .github and searches it in the same order. One file there covers every repo of the account that lacks its own.
Exception: LICENSE has no account-wide default. It must be in each repository so it travels with every clone, package and download.

blocks.md: GitHub makes the file hard to miss: when someone opens an issue or a pull request, they see a link to the contributing guidelines, and a repository with a `CONTRIBUTING.md` also gets a Contributing tab next to the README. So "I did not see the rules" is rarely a convincing excuse in a review thread.

A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

What a CONTRIBUTING file typically says, according to GitHub's own guidance: the steps for creating good issues or pull requests, links to external documentation, mailing lists or a code of conduct, and community and behavioural expectations. In practice it also tells you how to build and test, the commit message format, whether a sign-off is required, and which channel to use for questions.

Before investing time, the Open Source Guides also suggest checking that the project is alive: does it have a license, do maintainers respond to issues and pull requests, are issues getting closed, and were PRs merged recently? A great contribution to an abandoned project still gets no response.

Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

blocks.question: An org keeps CONTRIBUTING.md only in its public `.github` repository. Repo `org/tool` has `docs/CONTRIBUTING.md`. Which file does GitHub link when you open a PR on `org/tool`?
options: The org-wide file, because the .github repository always takes precedence
`docs/CONTRIBUTING.md`, because the repository's own file wins over the account default
Neither: the file must be in the repository root to be linked
Both are shown, merged into one page
blocks.explain: The account-level `.github` repository is a fallback used only when the repository has no file of that type. The repository's own file in `.github/`, root, or `docs/` wins, checked in that order.

blocks.question: Which community health file can NOT be provided as an account-wide default from the `.github` repository?
options: CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
SECURITY.md
Issue templates
LICENSE
blocks.explain: GitHub's docs say you cannot create a default license file: it must live in each repository so it is included when the project is cloned, packaged or downloaded. Defaults in the `.github` repository are not part of clones.

lessons.title: Issue first: when to ask, how to report, how to claim work

blocks.md: An **issue** is a public thread in the project's tracker. The Open Source Guides describe issues as starting a conversation and pull requests as starting work on a solution. You should usually open an issue to report an error you cannot solve yourself, to discuss a high-level idea, or to propose a new feature. You can go straight to a PR for small fixes (a typo, a broken link, an obvious error) or for work already agreed in an issue.

blocks.prompt: You spend a weekend writing a feature nobody asked for and open a 2,000-line PR. The code is good. What is the most likely outcome?
blocks.reveal: Often a polite close or no response at all. Maintainers must weigh whether the feature fits the project's direction and whether they want to maintain it for years, and a large unrequested change is expensive to review. The Open Source Guides' advice is direct: **if you want to make a substantial contribution, open an issue to ask before working on it.**

blocks.md: Why ask first? A simple model makes the tradeoff concrete. Say the work takes $H$ hours, and there is a probability $p$ that maintainers would decline the idea no matter how good the code is (out of scope, already planned differently, too costly to maintain). Writing an issue and reading the reply costs you about $c$ hours. If you skip the issue, you lose all $H$ hours with probability $p$.

blocks.tex: \mathbb{E}[\text{lost}_{\text{PR first}}] = pH \qquad \mathbb{E}[\text{lost}_{\text{issue first}}] \approx c \qquad \text{ask first when } H > \frac{c}{p}
blocks.caption: Simplified model: it assumes the issue reply reliably reveals a rejection, and ignores the design feedback you also get.

blocks.title: Expected hours lost: PR first vs issue first

scenes.caption: With p = 0.3 and c = 0.5 h, the lines cross at H = c/p = 1.67 h. For a 20 hour feature, PR first loses 6 h on average versus 0.5 h for asking.
An obvious bug fix has a low decline chance. At p = 0.05 the breakeven rises to 10 h, so a quick fix can go straight to a PR, as the guides suggest.
A big feature in a project with a firm roadmap: p = 0.5 and asking takes longer (c = 2 h). Breakeven is 4 h, so any real feature work should start with an issue.

blocks.title: Expected hours lost for three tasks (c = 0.5 h)

scenes.caption: A typo fix: H = 0.25 h, p = 0.05. PR first loses 0.01 h on average, asking costs 0.5 h. Just open the PR.
A bug fix: H = 4 h, p = 0.2. PR first loses 0.8 h on average, asking costs 0.5 h. Ask first.
A new feature: H = 20 h, p = 0.4. PR first loses 8.0 h on average, asking costs 0.5 h. Ask first.

blocks.md: Before opening anything, **search**: the README, the docs, and the issue tracker including *closed* issues. Duplicates cost triagers time. When you do file a bug, give context: what you tried, what happened, what you expected, and how to reproduce it. The guides contrast "X doesn't happen when I do Y" with "X is broken! Please fix it."

Many projects enforce structure with **issue forms**: YAML files in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` that render as a web form with required fields. A `config.yml` in the same folder controls the template chooser. Step through a small setup.

blocks.title: What an issue form and chooser config do
blocks.code:
# .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml
blank_issues_enabled: false
contact_links:
  - name: Security report
    url: https://example.org/security
    about: Please report vulnerabilities privately.

# .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml
name: Bug Report
description: File a bug report.
labels: ["bug", "triage"]
body:
  - type: textarea
    id: what-happened
    attributes:
      label: What happened?
    validations:
      required: true

scenes.caption: With blank issues disabled, people with Read or Triage roles see only the configured templates. Write, Maintain and Admin users still see a Blank issue option marked Maintainers only.
Contact links send some reports outside the tracker. A security link here steers vulnerabilities away from public issues.
Every issue form must include the top-level keys name, description and body. The name must be longer than 3 characters or the template is not shown.
Labels are applied automatically, so new reports land in the triage queue. A label that does not exist in the repo is not added.
A required textarea blocks submission until filled. On submit, answers are converted to Markdown in the issue body.
scenes.output:
### What happened?

The parser crashes on empty input.

blocks.md: To take on an existing issue, **comment that you are working on it** so others do not duplicate the work. If the issue is old, ask first whether it is still wanted. Maintainers often label beginner-friendly work `good first issue`; adding it makes GitHub more likely to surface the issue to newcomers, and appending `/contribute` to a repository URL lists them.

scenes.caption: You search open and closed issues, find nothing, and file a report through the form.
A maintainer confirms the bug and labels it. You comment to claim it, so nobody else starts the same fix.
Your PR description says Closes #37. GitHub links the two, so anyone reading the issue sees a fix in progress.
No review after a week? A polite public ping in the PR thread is fair. Do not email maintainers privately about it.
When the PR is merged into the default branch, the closing keyword closes issue #37 automatically.

blocks.md: Closing keywords (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`) only work when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**. Aimed at a release or feature branch, the keyword is ignored and the issue stays open after merge.

blocks.question: Your PR targets the `release-2.x` branch and its description says `Fixes #88`. It is merged. What happens to issue #88?
options: It closes, because Fixes is a closing keyword
It stays open, because keywords only act on PRs into the default branch
It closes only if you also wrote Fixes in the commit message
It is reopened automatically when the next release ships
blocks.explain: GitHub interprets closing keywords only when the PR targets the default branch. Otherwise no link is created and merging has no effect on the issue.

blocks.question: Using the model above, you want to fix a confusing error message (about 1 hour, decline chance about 0.1) and writing an issue costs about 0.5 hours. What is the sensible move?
options: Open an issue first: always ask before any code
Open the PR directly: expected loss 0.1 h is below the 0.5 h cost of asking
Do nothing: small fixes are not real contributions
Email the maintainer to ask privately
blocks.explain: Expected loss for PR first is $pH$ = 0.1 x 1 = 0.1 h, less than $c$ = 0.5 h, and the breakeven is $c/p$ = 5 h. Small, obvious fixes go straight to a PR, unless CONTRIBUTING says otherwise. Private email goes against the norm of public communication.

lessons.title: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder

blocks.md: A **code of conduct** (CoC) sets ground rules for behaviour and says how violations are handled. Most projects do not write one from scratch: they adopt a template, and the most widely used is the [Contributor Covenant](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/). Its version 2.1 has six sections: a pledge, standards (examples of good and unacceptable behaviour), enforcement responsibilities, scope, enforcement (where and how to report), and enforcement guidelines, plus an attribution note.

**Scope** matters more than people expect. Contributor Covenant 2.1 applies within all community spaces (issues, PRs, chat, forums, events) and also when someone officially represents the community in public, for example posting from an official account or acting as an appointed representative at an event. Community leaders may remove, edit or reject comments, commits, code, issues and other contributions that do not follow it.

scenes.caption: Reports go to the leaders named in the CoC, who must review them promptly and fairly and protect the reporter's privacy.
Correction: for unprofessional or unwelcome behaviour, such as inappropriate language. A private written warning explaining why; a public apology may be requested.
Warning: a single incident or series of actions. No interaction with the people involved for a set period, including on social media. Breaking that can lead to a ban.
Temporary Ban: a serious violation, including sustained inappropriate behaviour. No interaction or public communication with the community for a set period.
Permanent Ban: a pattern of violations, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward classes of people. Dashed arrows show escalation when earlier terms are broken.

blocks.md: Leaders choose the level by community impact, not strictly in order: a single serious violation can go straight to a temporary ban. The 2.1 text credits Mozilla's enforcement ladder as the inspiration. Version 3.0 of the Covenant reframes the section as **addressing and repairing harm**, with a ladder of Warning, Temporarily Limited Activities, Temporary Suspension and Permanent Ban, and suggested repair steps at every level below Permanent Ban (which allows no repair). It also says lower rungs may be skipped for severe violations.

A CoC is not only about insults. Contributor Covenant 2.1 lists publishing others' private information (an address, an email) without explicit permission as unacceptable, and it covers private harassment too.

Two kinds of reports should **not** go in a public issue: conduct reports and security vulnerabilities. A CoC names its own contact (the template has a placeholder for the project to fill in). For vulnerabilities, read `SECURITY.md`, which tells you the supported versions and how to report. Some repositories also enable GitHub's **private vulnerability reporting**: a Report a vulnerability button on the Security and quality tab that sends the report only to maintainers.

blocks.title: Routing a report to the right channel

scenes.caption: Ordinary bugs and feature ideas belong in public, where others can learn from and join the discussion.
A vulnerability in a public issue tells attackers before users can patch. Follow SECURITY.md; if there is no policy and no private reporting, open an issue asking only for a security contact.
Conduct problems go to the people named in the CoC, who must protect the reporter's privacy. The Open Source Guides allow private contact for exactly these two cases.

blocks.md: Default to public communication, with two exceptions: security vulnerabilities and serious conduct violations. Each has its own documented private channel; find it before you need it.

blocks.question: You find a way to read other users' files through a project's upload endpoint. The repo has SECURITY.md and private vulnerability reporting enabled. What do you do?
options: Open a detailed public issue so the fix gets attention quickly
Open a PR with the fix and describe the exploit in the PR body
Use the private report (or the channel SECURITY.md names) and follow its instructions
Post a minimal reproducer in the project's public chat
blocks.explain: Public issues, PRs and chat disclose the vulnerability before a fix ships. SECURITY.md gives the project's reporting instructions, and private vulnerability reporting delivers the report only to maintainers.

blocks.question: Under Contributor Covenant 2.1, a contributor gets a Warning with a 30-day no-contact period. A week later they message the person who reported them on social media to explain themselves. What follows?
options: Nothing: social media is outside the project's spaces
It breaks the Warning's terms, which cover external channels like social media, and can lead to a temporary or permanent ban
It is allowed because the contributor is apologising
The Warning is cancelled and replaced by a Correction
blocks.explain: A Warning forbids interaction with the people involved for a set period, including unsolicited contact and external channels like social media. The text says violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

lessons.title: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not

blocks.md: The newest section of many CONTRIBUTING files is a policy on AI tools. Projects started writing them because tools make it cheap to produce a patch but do not make it cheaper to review one. The policies differ a lot, so you must read the one for each project. Three real examples span the range.

blocks.title: Three AI policies on one spectrum

nodes.label:
shared concern: review
time and accountability

scenes.caption: QEMU declines any contribution believed to include or derive from AI generated content. Using AI to research APIs, debug or run static analysis is fine if the output is not in the patch.
The kernel asks for transparency: say which tools produced meaningful content, add an Assisted-by tag, and AI agents must never add Signed-off-by. Maintainers may still reject.
LLVM allows any tool, but a human must review all output before asking for review, must be able to answer questions, and should label substantial tool use.
All three come back to the same point: a person must stand behind every line, because review is the scarce resource and legal certification needs a human.

blocks.md: **QEMU's reasoning is legal.** QEMU requires a Signed-off-by line certifying the Developer's Certificate of Origin (DCO), the statement you met in the previous course that you have the right to submit the code under the project's license. QEMU's policy says the copyright and license status of AI output is ill-defined, so contributors cannot reliably make that certification, and the project will decline a contribution if AI use is known or suspected. It notes the policy may evolve as the legal situation is clarified.

**LLVM's reasoning is about review cost.** Its policy calls unreviewed LLM output sent to maintainers an **extractive contribution**: one whose cost to review and merge is greater than its benefit to the project (a term taken from Nadia Eghbal's book *Working in Public*). The golden rule: a contribution should be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review it.

LLVM's concrete rules, from its [AI Tool Use Policy](https://llvm.org/docs/AIToolPolicy.html):

- Read and review all generated code or text before asking anyone to review it. You are the author and fully accountable.
- Label substantial tool-generated content in the PR description or commit message, for instance with an `Assisted-by:` trailer.
- Writing the PR description yourself is strongly recommended (tools for translation or copy-editing are fine).
- No agents that act in project spaces without human approval, and no bots posting unreviewed review comments.
- Do not use AI tools to fix issues labelled `good first issue`: those exist so newcomers learn.

blocks.title: A commit message that follows a disclose-style policy
blocks.code:
parser: reject empty input instead of crashing

An empty file reached tokenize() with a null buffer
and crashed. Return a clear error before tokenizing.

I used an LLM to draft the regression test, then
rewrote and ran it; the fix itself is mine.

Fixes: #37
Assisted-by: <tool name>
Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@example.org>

scenes.caption: Subject and body are written by the human: what changed and why. LLVM strongly recommends you write the description yourself.
Say what the tool did and what you checked. The kernel's guidelines ask which tools were used, which portions they affected, and how the change was tested.
Assisted-by labels substantial tool use. The exact format is project specific: the kernel defines its own, LLVM only gives Assisted-by as an example. Check the project's docs.
Signed-off-by is a human's legal DCO certification. The kernel says AI agents must not add it. At QEMU, this same commit would be declined because AI content is included.

blocks.md: Common misconception: "I reviewed it, so I do not need to mention the tool." Under LLVM's policy review is required **and** substantial tool use should still be labelled. Under QEMU's policy, reviewing it does not help: AI-generated content is declined. The rules are per project.

How maintainers respond also differs. LLVM maintainers paste a standard comment asking for justification, may apply an `extractive` label, and can escalate to moderators to lock the conversation. The kernel says maintainers may treat a tool-assisted patch like any other, reject it outright, or review it with extra scrutiny or lower priority. The [Open Source Guides](https://opensource.guide/how-to-contribute/) give the general rule: verify the output is accurate, follows project conventions and addresses the issue, because you remain responsible.

Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

blocks.question: An LLVM issue is labelled `good first issue`. You can fix it in two minutes with a coding agent and you will carefully review the result. Is that allowed under LLVM's policy?
options: Yes, as long as you review the output and add Assisted-by
No: AI tools must not be used to fix good first issues, which exist as learning opportunities
Yes, but only if a maintainer approves the agent first
No, because LLVM bans all AI tools
blocks.explain: LLVM generally allows tools with a human in the loop, but makes a specific exception: AI tools must not be used for issues labelled good first issue, since automating them squanders the learning opportunity.

blocks.question: Why does QEMU decline AI-generated patches even when the contributor fully understands and tests them?
options: Because AI code is always lower quality
Because it cannot be reviewed on a mailing list
Because the contributor cannot confidently certify the DCO when the copyright and license status of AI output is unsettled
Because QEMU forbids all tools, including static analysis
blocks.explain: QEMU's concern is provenance: the Signed-off-by line certifies the DCO, and with unclear licensing of AI output the project will not take the legal risk. It explicitly allows AI use for research, debugging and static analysis whose output is not in the patch.

blocks.question: Which action breaks the Linux kernel's guidance for AI coding assistants?
options: Adding an Assisted-by tag
Letting the assistant add a Signed-off-by line to the commit
Writing a reproducer before sending a bug fix
Stating in the changelog which tool found the bug
blocks.explain: Only humans can legally certify the DCO, so AI agents must not add Signed-off-by. The human submitter reviews the code, adds their own sign-off and takes responsibility. The other three are things the guidance asks for.
